# Introduction

Throughout the semester, we will use a combination of computational tools. This a summary of the main tools:

-   **Command line:** primarily to interact with git, install programs and run a few scripts

-   **Python3:** for programming taks

-   **Git/GitHub:** for version control, reproucibility and for sharing materials

-   **Jupyter Notebooks:** as a main IDE to work with Python

-   **Quarto via RStudio:** as a secondary IDE (you can make your primary if you prefer) to coding in Python/R/SQL


Let's cover how to set up each of these tools in your local machines.

::: callout-warning
If you run into issues, please set up an office hours appointment for assistance
:::

## Command Line

At times, we'll use a unix-based command line. The command line will feature into our discussion on using `git` and also running Python programs. If you use a Mac or a Linux operating system, then a functioning command line comes with your operating system. For Apple machines, this is the **Terminal**.

For Windows (specifically Windows 10), you can enable Linux Bash shell. The following offers a [tutorial](https://www.howtogeek.com/249966/how-to-install-and-use-the-linux-bash-shell-on-windows-10/) on how to do this.

If you're using a version of Windows that pre-dates version 10, then [Git Bash](https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/git-bash#:~:text=Git%20Bash%20is%20an%20application,operating%20system%20through%20written%20commands.) offers a program will allow you to use `git` commands from your windows machine.

Later in the first class, we will cover some concepts of working with the command line. You can get a full notebook with a intro to command line in the materials for week 1

## Python3

We'll use Python3 throughout this course. Below are instructions for downloading Python3 using command line packages manager (`Homebrew` for mac, `Chocolatey` for windows).

-   [Installing Python3 using Homebrew on a Mac (Apple)](https://docs.python-guide.org/starting/install3/osx/)

-   [Installing Python3 using Chocolatey on a PC (Windows)](https://python-docs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/starting/install3/win.html)

An alternative way to install Python3 is to download an [**Anaconda** distribution](https://www.anaconda.com/products/individual). I will use `pip` rather than `conda` in the instruction for downloading Python modules. These are simply two ways of downloading and managing open-source software packages. **Choose which ever works best for you**

Some computers already have python3 installed. You can check if that is your case through your command line

``` markdown
python3 --version
```

On some versions of Windows, you may need to use py instead of python3:

``` markdown
py --version
```

In either case, the output of this command should be something like Python 3.9.13 

## Jupyter Notebooks

Once you have Python3 on your computer, you can install a Jupyter Notebook. If you downloaded Python3 using Anaconda, then Jupyter Notebook comes with the distribution and requires no further installation on your part. If you are not using Anaconda, you can install Jupyter notebook running the following code using your command line.

``` markdown
# on your command line
pip install jupyter
```

You can then activate a Jupyter Notebook from the command line by typing:

``` markdown
# on your command line
jupyter notebook
```

### Workflow to work with Jupyter Notebooks

Here is my workflow to open Jupyter Notebooks using the commandline.

1.  Open the terminal

2.  Navigate (using `cd`) to the folder you want to be the root of your jupyter notebook

3.  Open the notebook (`jupyter notebook`)

It looks like this if I were to open a notebook in the folder I have for this course

``` markdown
# open terminal
cd ppol_5203_fall2026
jupyter notebook
```

### Workflow with Anaconda.

If you installed Python using Anaconda distribution system (here: https://www.anaconda.com/products/individual). You can open Jupyter through a point-and-click system.

In the lecture notes, you can also find a Introduction to Jupyter notebook. We will cover this in the first class of the course.

## Rstudio + Reticulate\|Quarto

In your classes that are focused on using `R`, `RStudio` will be your main IDE. However, `RStudio` isn't just for `R`. It can handle a number of different languages. We can use Python in `RStudio` using the `reticulate` package.

Here's a notebook to teach you how to use Python in Rstudio. Check out [the intro to quarto notebook](lecture_notes/week-1/intro_to_quarto.qmd). Let's cover some of the installation steps here:

1. To install `RStudio`, [download from the following link](https://www.rstudio.com/products/rstudio/download/) . `reticulate` is an R package that allows one run a Python REPL in the R console. In addition, it allows one to read in and use Python code, and pass data between R and and Python. The following provides [instructions on installing `reticulate`](https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/).

2. With `reticulate`, you can use Rstudio as a IDE for Python. Another option is to use Quarto (the next-generation version of R Markdown) as an unified framework to generate notebooks with text + code. If you're an R Markdown user, you will see how Quarto is just an extension of the capabilities that were previously provided by R Markdown. Now, instead of `.rmd` files, we have `.qmd` files. Quarto is already installed with RStudio.
